/-!
# Erdős Problem 371

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/371](https://www.erdosproblems.com/371)
-/

namespace Erdos371

/--
Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$. Show that the set of $n$
with $P(n+1) > P(n)$ has density $\frac{1}{2}$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_371 :
    { n | Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) > Nat.maxPrimeFac n }.HasDensity (1/2) := by
  sorry

-- TODO: add the statements from the additional material
end Erdos371

reformulations.difference: Lean includes all natural numbers, with maxPrimeFac 0 = 0 and maxPrimeFac 1 = 1, whereas the literature uses positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n > 1, maxPrimeFac is precisely the greatest prime divisor; its value at 1 agrees with Wang’s convention P⁺(1)=1. Including 0 changes the counting function by only one. More generally, deleting n < K changes normalized counts by a fixed constant divided by N, which tends to zero. In /workspace/review/invariance.lean I proved S.HasDensity d ↔ (S ∩ Set.Ici K).HasDensity d and instantiated it for this set with K=1 and K=2. The proof does not depend on sorryAx or the conjecture.

review.notes: The sole declaration faithfully states the conjecture. HasDensity is the full natural-density limit relative to all of ℕ, and 1/2 elaborates in ℝ. Counting n<N instead of 1≤n≤N changes normalized counts by O(1/N). Checked the helper definitions, proved their relevant semantics, and computed small cases and counts through N=1000. Both scratch files compile successfully. The cited website still records the problem as open; its logarithmic-density and conditional results do not settle this statement. Direct website access was blocked, so its reader view supplied status and remarks, while Wang’s LaTeX supplied the exact formula.
